## Introduction

Welcome to the Pacific Salmon Commission RTMB course `RTMB (Template Model Builder in R) and Maximum Likelihood Estimation in R`. In this course we expect you to be experienced writing code in R, be able to turn a likelihood equation into code, and then find the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE). In this pre-workshop module, we will make sure that you can achieve this while also setting you up with code that you are familiar with that we can build into an RTMB script.

## Data

We will start with some sockeye stock recruit data from the Fraser River. There are a total of 19 stocks to consider. We will use up to year 2020 and values are in millions of fish. Let's load in the data.

```{r, warning = FALSE, eval = FALSE}
sox <- read.csv("../data/sockeye/SRDATA2026 1.csv")
stock <- read.csv("../data/sockeye/FC_StockInfo 2.csv")
sox <- sox |> merge(stock, by = "PopID")

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(data = sox, aes(x = log(eff), y = log(rec), colour = PopNmL)) + geom_point() + theme_bw() + xlab("Log Spawners") + ylab("Log Recruits")
```


We will start with a Ricker stock recruit model, defined by female spawners, $S_{kt}$, for brood year $t$ and stock $k$, which produce $R_{kt}$ recruits. Recruits are the sum over multiple return years and age classes. Assuming some Gaussian white noise $\epsilon_{kt} \sim Normal(0, \sigma^2)$,

$$
  R_{kt} = S_{kt} \exp(\alpha_{kt} -\beta_k S_{k,t} + \epsilon_{k,t}),
$$
where $\alpha_{kt}$ is log productivity and $\beta_k$ is carrying capacity. This is usually written as the log recruits per spawners,

$$
  \log(R_{kt}/S_{kt}) =\alpha_{kt} - \beta_k S_{k,t} + \epsilon_{k,t}.
$$
We can fit a version of this model in R using just the `lm` function.
```{r, eval = FALSE}
sox <- sox |> within(logRS <- log(rec/eff))
fit <- lm(logRS ~ 0 + PopNmL + eff:PopNmL, data = sox)
# summary(fit)
```

To write our own version of `lm` to fit this model we need to know a few things. 

1. Computation must occur on the log scale. This is because multiplying lots of small probabilities together creates a very small number, which leads to numerical underflow. However, the log of a small number is just a negative big number. As a result, summing the log likelihood is the important part.
1. Numerical optimization functions typically work with the negative log likelihood so we want to return a negative log likelihood.
1. The optimizer will expect a single input of the parameters as a vector.
1. The coefficient terms can be any number but the standard deviation $\sigma$ is strictly positive. This requires a transformation, typically fitting the parameter on the $log$ scale, or $\theta = \log(\sigma)$, to ensure that it is strictly positive.

Please write a general function for a stock recruit model that can take any covariate input for $\alpha$ and $\beta$. To help you with this consider writing things as a design matrix `X` and use a wee bit of linear algebra to compute.
```{r, eval = FALSE}
  X <- model.matrix(~0 + PopNmL + eff:PopNmL, data = sox)
  alpha_beta <- rnorm(ncol(X))
  ## Version 1: Linear Algebra
  exp_logRS <- X %*% alpha_beta
  dim(exp_logRS)
  
  ## Version 2: Looping
  exp_logRS <- numeric(nrow(X))
  for(i in 1:nrow(X)) exp_logRS[i] <- sum(X[i,] * alpha_beta)
```

To help you get started, see below a very basic example of finding the mean of some normally distributed data.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
set.seed(1)
dat <- rnorm(50)

fit0_lm <- lm(dat~1)

negll <- function(pars, data){
  mu <- pars[1]
  sigma <- exp(pars[2])
  -sum(dnorm(data, mu, sigma, log = TRUE))
}

pars_init <- c(0,0)
fit0 <- nlminb(pars_init, negll, data = dat)
fit0$par[1] - mean(dat) ## Should be the same...
fit0$par[1] - coef(fit0_lm)
exp(fit0$par[2]) - sd(dat) ## Different!!
exp(fit0$par[2]) - sigma(fit0_lm)
```
Notice here that the MLE for the mean is exactly the mean of the data. But, the standard deviation is not the same as our sigma parameter! That's because the MLE of sigma is a biased variance estimator. We must do a bias correction for them to match ($n/(n-1)$).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
n <- length(dat)
exp(fit0$par[2])*sqrt(n/(n-1)) - sigma(fit0_lm)
```

We will discuss a lot of these concepts within the course. But for those who want to take this further, we will now estimate the uncertainty of the parameter. To do this, we can use the inverse of the hessian of the negative log likelihood. This sounds super complicated but the Hessian is the matrix of second derivatives, and describes the curvature around the MLE and thus variance, or at least in a very hand wavy way. This gets more complicated for parameter transformations and will be discussed in detail in the course.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
H <- numDeriv::hessian(negll, fit0$par, data = dat)
V <- solve(H)
## 95% CI for mu: Note that the test statistic is t, not z.
## We know the exact distribution of the parameter, so don't approximate it
## using a normal (i.e. 1.96).
fit0$par[1] + c(-1,1)*qt(1 - 0.05 / 2, df = n - 1)*sqrt(V[1,1])
confint(fit0_lm)
```
